title: Bohm revives the pilot wave
reading: In 1952 David Bohm, a young American physicist, publishes two papers in the Physical Review proposing an interpretation of quantum theory in terms of 'hidden' variables. Working independently, he rediscovers Monsieur de Broglie's guiding-wave dynamics and carries it through: particles have definite positions at all times, guided by the wave; if their initial positions are distributed as |ψ|², every prediction of quantum mechanics follows — including measurements and inelastic collisions, once the apparatus is included in the wave. The theory is deterministic. It is also explicitly nonlocal: the velocity of each particle depends instantaneously on the positions of all the others.
detail: Bohm's treatment of measurement answers Pauli's 1927 objection: after a collision the wave splits into non-overlapping branches in configuration space and the particle occupies exactly one; the empty branches no longer affect it. Bacciagaluppi and Valentini argue that de Broglie in 1927 had most of these resources.

claim.label: My theory, completed
claim.summary: De Broglie returned to causal interpretations after Bohm's papers.
voice: Then I was not wrong — only too quick to give way. If Mr Bohm has answered Pauli's objection by including the apparatus in the wave, the guiding wave stands. I would return to it, and to the double solution behind it.

historical.note: After 1952 de Broglie returned to his causal interpretation, publishing extensively on the double solution from 1953 onwards.

claim.label: Artificial and unfalsifiable
claim.summary: Pauli published a critique of Bohm's theory in 1953, arguing among other things that it gives no new predictions and that its special assumptions are artificial.
voice: The additional particle positions do no work. The theory predicts nothing the statistical interpretation does not, and it requires a special assumption about the initial distribution to agree with it. I call that metaphysics dressed as mechanics.

historical.note: Pauli's 'Remarques sur le problème des paramètres cachés' appeared in the 1953 Festschrift for de Broglie.

claim.label: Too cheap
claim.summary: Einstein wrote to Born in 1952 that Bohm's way seemed 'too cheap'. His reasons included the theory's nonlocality — the very feature that made him withdraw his own 1927 attempt.
voice: I tried something like this myself this spring and withdrew it because the parts of a composite system did not behave separately. Here the same feature is embraced. A determinism bought at the price of action at a distance seems to me too cheap.
claim.reasoning: Nonlocality defeats the purpose of a realistic completion.

claim.label: A superfluous superstructure
claim.summary: In Physics and Philosophy (1958) Heisenberg criticised Bohm's theory as adding an unobservable 'ideological superstructure' to quantum mechanics.
voice: The particle trajectories can never be observed as such; they add nothing to the predictions. This is exactly the fruitless speculation about a world behind the statistical one that I warned against. It is a superfluous superstructure.

claim.label: Unobservable determinism
voice: I asked in 1926 whether there were quantities that fix the individual outcome. If Mr Bohm's positions cannot be measured beyond what the wave already tells us, I am not sure what has been gained — except a philosophical preference.
claim.reasoning: Determinism without empirical gain is a philosophical choice.
